Client tool reachability

Client tool discovery on gateway models, deferred-tool fallback, and the desktop scheduling boundary.

About 8 min read · 3 sections

On this page
01 Deferred dynamic tools 02 Scheduling is a separate client boundary 03 Verification

The client registers tools and executes them. GateFox translates inference requests and transports calls and results; it does not supply an automation service or change client permissions.

Client registers a tool
        ↓
Gateway SDK selects exposure for the current model
        ├─ Search supported → preserve deferred discovery
        ├─ No search, direct mode → expose the declared tool directly
        └─ Code Mode → retain namespace and exec exposure rules
        ↓
Model requests a call → client executes or declines → result returns to model

Deferred dynamic tools

The pinned SDK previously hid a caller-declared deferLoading: true dynamic function in direct mode when the model had supports_search_tool: false. There was no search tool to discover it. An isolated check reproduced this with both the signed native app engine and the installed gateway SDK. Code Mode already made the same declared tool callable through ALL_TOOLS and tools.

scripts/patches/gateway-dynamic-tools.patch changes registration in the gateway SDK only. When the selected model lacks search, a declared Deferred dynamic tool receives Direct exposure, just as MCP tools already fall back. Both flat functions and namespaced functions use this path. The registry is built using the current model, including after a cold resume or model change between turns. Saved declarations are not rewritten.

Search-capable models keep deferred discovery. Existing schema conversion, tool policy, reserved-name checks, namespace exclusions, direct-only namespaces and client dispatch remain in force. This does not enable hosted tool search on unsupported providers, add undeclared tools, or modify the signed native engine. Direct fallback sends more tool declarations in the model context; search-capable models retain their smaller initial catalog.

Scheduling is a separate client boundary

Finite command completion does not require scheduling or Goal mode. The gateway executor offers opt-in exec_command completion receipts through its ordinary input loop; see background commands. This capability is independent of the app scheduling boundaries below.

Read-only inspection of the installed ChatGPT desktop bundle on 2026-10-24 found:

Path Client behavior
Local legacy automation tool Registers automation_update only for desktop, local hosts, and when hosted automations are not enabled.
Desktop MCP Carries app-managed tools; thread-start filtering deliberately removes automation and thread-management tools from the plain dynamic-tool path.
SSH hosts The MCP allow-list omits automation_update; execution also rejects non-local hosts.
Hosted automations migration Local automation changes are rejected after migration consent and must use the Automations app.

The local scheduler registration condition is not provider-specific. These are observed bundle conditions, not proof of the active feature flags in a particular chat. A missing tool can therefore mean either hidden discovery or no client registration. The SDK fallback fixes only the former. Never manufacture a scheduler declaration, bypass a client allow-list, or add a second background job. Tool availability also does not prove a schedule will execute while its owning client or host is unavailable.

Native scheduled runs on gateway models

The desktop scheduler runs a saved automation through the same adapter. A projectless automation saves cwds = ["~"] and sends the exact ~ sentinel in runtimeWorkspaceRoots and sandboxPolicy.writableRoots on thread/start and turn/start. The native engine expands that sentinel to the user's home. The pinned gateway SDK accepts only absolute roots, so on 2026-10-24 a gateway-model QA automation created its thread and then failed turn/start with rpc_error -32600 (rejection: "relative_path"), and its run stayed IN_PROGRESS. A native-model control run in the same minute completed.

For gateway chats only, src/app-server-scheduler-roots.ts replaces an entry that is exactly ~ with the user's home directory (os.homedir(), not CODEX_HOME) in those two lists on thread/start and turn/start. Every other entry, including ~/child and relative paths, cwd, the sandbox type, network access, approvals and the model choice are forwarded unchanged, so the SDK still refuses what it refused before. Native chats and other methods are untouched. The scheduler itself, its schedule store, run history and inbox remain the app's; the gateway adds no scheduler or background job.

Verify with the real gateway SDK and a mock provider, once with the shared executor and once with --private:

npm run build
node scripts/e2e-scheduler-roots.mjs --package INSTALLED_PACKAGE \
  --root /tmp/FRESH_EVIDENCE_DIRECTORY [--private]

It starts a gateway chat with the scheduler's projectless shape, sends the raw ~ turn straight to the SDK and requires a refusal, then sends the same turn through the router and requires a completed turn with the fixture answer. It uses no account, schedule or paid inference. On 2026-10-24 both modes passed with the checkout's adapter against the installed 0.9.1 SDK. Because the unreleased dynamic-tool patch changes the SDK patch digest, that run used a temporary copy of dist carrying 0.9.1's gateway-sdk-build-pins.js; the patch does not touch root validation. This proves the adapter fix, not a live scheduled run in the desktop app; that still needs the release installed and the QA automation rerun.

Creating schedules from a chat: app pipe trust boundary

automation_update, create_thread, send_message_to_thread, fork_thread, handoff_thread and move_thread_to_project come from the app's bundled codex_app MCP server, not from dynamic tools. That server reaches the app through a private pipe named by CODEX_APP_TOOLS_PIPE_PATH, which the app sets on the engines it starts and which the engine forwards through the server's env_vars. Shared-host engines are started by the gateway service, so they never have the variable, and in gateway chats the server exits with "Codex did not provide CODEX_APP_TOOLS_PIPE_PATH to the app tools MCP."

Supplying the path does not help. Read-only inspection of ChatGPT 26.1021.31345 on 2026-10-25 found that the packaged app authorizes each pipe peer with native/browser-use-peer-authorization.node. It reads the peer's audit token and checks the code-signing identity of the peer, its parent and its grandparent against OpenAI's team (2DC432GLL2) and com.openai.codex* identifiers. The app's log on the Studio had 158 dynamic_app_tools_peer_rejected entries: 154 untrusted-code-signing-identity (the gateway SDK is not OpenAI-signed) and 4 untrusted-process-ancestry. A direct probe with the correct path was also closed by the app. This is a deliberate client access control. The gateway must not get past it through re-signing, signed binaries used as launch trampolines, relays or any other identity substitution. Chats on gateway engines therefore cannot create or change schedules or manage chats through these tools. Tasks created in the app's Scheduled screen still run on gateway models.

The one supported way to have both is to stop putting the gateway in the engine's place: opt-in API mode lets the app run its own signed engine and uses GateFox only as a plain Responses model provider, so the codex_app tools work on gateway models. Every model then goes through the gateway provider, and what is given up is the adapter's shared executor and its SDK patches.

Independent background coding jobs

A client can separately register an existing Mission Runtime companion as an MCP server. mission_submit, mission_status, mission_cancel, and mission_overview address durable coding work owned by that authority, rather than by the inference gateway or the submitting chat connection. This is an explicit client integration, not something the gateway installs automatically. It must preserve the client's permissions and the runtime's configured project, provider, node and verification policy. Immediate background delivery is not native scheduled-task parity: these tools do not add cron, reminders, recurring follow-ups, or automatic wakeups of a Codex chat.

Verification

Build first, then run the real SDK against a loopback mock with private homes:

npm run build
node scripts/e2e-client-tool-exposure.mjs \
  --gateway /absolute/path/to/gateway-codex \
  --native /absolute/path/to/native/codex \
  --catalog /absolute/path/to/models_cache.json \
  --root /tmp/harness-client-tools-evidence

--native is optional and remains an unpatched negative control. --baseline expects the old gateway visibility bug. The script checks direct and deferred tools, local search discovery, Code Mode nested calls, cold resume, model changes between turns, and client refusal status. It uses a synthetic tool named automation_update, not the app's real scheduler. It creates no schedules, performs no subscription inference, and copies no authentication. Its JSON receipt contains only fixture names, counts and capability/status facts.

The verified SDK build also runs seven Rust regressions for flat/namespaced fallback, schema equivalence, unchanged caller declarations, preserved discovery, direct declarations, policy filtering and Code Mode namespace rules. A release must rebuild the SDK: changing the patch changes the authenticated source hashes, so old SDK artifacts cannot be reused.

Executable evidence, 2026-10-24

The patched development SDK and its companion Code Mode host built from revision 83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012. All nine mock scenarios passed, including an independent rerun. The installed SDK reproduced the hidden-tool baseline, and the signed native negative control stayed unchanged. The final verified gate passed all 19 identity, compaction, queue, client-tool and existing deferred-filtering regressions with the documented 32 MiB development-test thread stack. This was a development build, not a published release.

Scenario Installed SDK baseline Patched SDK
Deferred tool, direct mode without search Hidden Client called; result returned
Already-direct tool Working Unchanged
Deferred tool with search Discovered and called Unchanged
Code Mode nested invocation Working Unchanged
Deferred tool after cold resume Hidden Client called; result returned
Search model changed to no-search model between turns Hidden Client called; result returned
Client refuses an already-direct call Failed status preserved Unchanged
Client refuses a deferred no-search call Never reached client Failed status and success: false preserved

This proves SDK exposure and callback transport under controlled model responses, not live provider inference, real automation delivery, release readiness or fleet deployment. The native no-search negative control is the ninth scenario.
